title: Tesla's Missing Autopilot Data Showed It Detected A Hazard Before Fatal Crash, Despite Claims It Was Missing

reading.body:
A Tesla vehicle with Autopilot engaged struck a parked car in 2024, killing one person. During the resulting lawsuit, Tesla told the family that crash data was unavailable, but a security researcher recovered the data through Tesla's bug bounty program, proving the vehicle's systems had detected a hazard before impact. The data contradicted Tesla's assertion that the information did not exist.

This is a failure of disclosure during litigation. The deployment failure itself—the Autopilot system's behavior in the crash—was investigated through data that Tesla initially claimed was inaccessible. A human review of available data before making statements to the family, or a documented data retention protocol, would have prevented the discrepancy. A jury found Tesla partially liable and a judge upheld a verdict of $243 million in damages.

It is not established whether Tesla's claim that data was missing resulted from system design, data deletion practices, or other causes.

summary:
# Summary

Tesla faced legal consequences after a self-driving vehicle struck a parked car in 2024, killing one person and injuring another. During the lawsuit, Tesla claimed it had no crash data available, but a hacker working through Tesla's bug bounty program recovered the information, proving the company did possess the footage. A jury determined Tesla was partially responsible, and in February 2026, a judge upheld the verdict, requiring the company to pay $243 million in damages. Tesla subsequently renamed its Autopilot and Full Self Driving features to clarify that human supervision is required.

The incident raises concerns about Tesla's upcoming Cybercab launch, fully autonomous vehicles without manual controls. Data shows Tesla vehicles with active driver-assist systems were involved in 207 crashes in May, a record high. Investigators are examining potential failures in the self-driving software, and recent high-profile accidents, including one involving San Francisco 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan, highlight ongoing safety issues. Questions remain about Tesla's transparency regarding crash data and vehicle safety performance as the company prepares to deploy fully autonomous robotaxis.
